'''Alauda''' (a-lâ′dä̤), ''n.''   [L., the lark; according to Pliny, Suetonius, and Gregory of Tours, a {{img float|file=century v01 p0155 c1f2.png|width=222px|align=left|cap={{smaller|Woodlark (''Alauda arborea'').}}}} Gaulish or Celtic word (cf. Bret. ''alchoueder'', ''alchouedez'', the lark); said to be “lit. ‘great songstress,’ from ''al'', high or great, and ''aud'', song.” The W. name ''uchedydd'', lit. ‘soarer,’ is a different word. Hence It. ''aloda'' = Sp. ''alondra'', OSp. ''aluda'', ''aloa'' = Pr. ''alauza'' = OF. ''aloe'', with dim. ML. ''laudula'', ''laudila'', It. ''allodola'', ''lodola'' (dial. ''lodana''), and OIt. ''alodetta'', ''allodetta'' = OSp. ''aloeta'' = Pr. ''alauzeta'' = F. ''alouette'', the lark. Cf. ''calandra'' and ''lark''1.]   A genus of birds, typical of the family ''Alaudidæ'', or larks. {{smaller|The genus was formerly coextensive with the family, but is now restricted to such species as the skylark, ''A. arvensis'', and the woodlark, ''A. arborea''. The species of ''Alauda'' proper are natives of the old world, and inhabit chiefly its northern portions; they are small, plain-colored, spotted, and streaked birds; they nest on the ground, and are noted for singing as they soar aloft, and for the delicacy of their flesh. See ''Alaudidæ'' and ''lark''1.}} '''Alaudidæ''' (a-lâ′di-dē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Alauda'' + ''-idæ''.]   The lark family; a family of birds, of the order ''Passeres'' and suborder ''Oscines''. {{smaller|They are notably distinguished from other oscine ''Passeres'' by having the tarsi scutellate behind, and are therefore referred by some to a special series, ''Oscines scutelliplantares'', in distinction from most other ''Oscines'', which are laminiplantar. By others, however, the ''Alaudidæ'' have been ranked as a subfamily, ''Alaudinæ'', under ''Fringillidæ''. The hallux bears a lengthened straightened claw. There are many genera and species, mostly of the old world, and especially of Africa; only one genus, ''Eremophila'' or ''Otocorys'', the shore or horned lark, is indigenous to America. The ''Alaudidæ'' are mostly migratory; they inhabit open country, nest on the ground, lay colored eggs, and sing as they soar; some of the species are gregarious. See ''Alauda'' and ''lark''1.}} '''Alaudinæ''' (al-â-dī′nē), ''n. pl.''   [NL., < ''Alauda'' + ''-inæ''.]   A subfamily of larks. {{smaller|The term represents—(''a'') A subfamily of ''Fringillidæ'', including all larks. [Disused.] (''b'') A subfamily of ''Alaudidæ'', including the typical larks represented by the genus ''Alauda'' and its immediate allies.}} '''alaudine''' (a-lâ′din), ''a.''   [< ''Alauda'' + ''-ine''1.]   Having the character of a lark; pertaining to the ''Alaudidæ'' or lark family. {{smaller block|There is . . . abundant evidence of the susceptibility of the ''Alaudine'' structure to modification from external circumstances. {{right|''Encyc. Brit.'', XIV. 316.}}}} '''alaun†''', '''alaund†''', '''alaunt†''', ''n.'' Same as ''alan''. '''Alaus''' (a-lā′us), ''n.''   [NL., in form < Gr. ἀλαός, blind, < ἀ- priv. + λάειν, see; but said to be based on ἀλᾶσθαι, wander, roam, stray.]   A genus of click-beetles, of the family ''Elateridæ.'' ''A. oculatus,'' one of the largest of the North American snapping-beetles, is a well-known species upward of 1½ inches long. It has two velvety black spots encircled with white on the prothorax, and white dots scattered over the whole surface; its larvæ live in decaying wood. [[File:century v01 p0155 c1f3.png|center|269px]] {{c|{{smaller|Alb of Thomas à Becket in the cathedral at Sens, with apparels of rich stuff sewed on the bottom and sleeves.}}}} '''Alausa''' (a-lâ′sä), ''n.'' In the ''Rom. Cath. Ch.'' (and in many Anglican churches), a white linen robe, with tight sleeves, worn at the celebration of the eucharist under the chasuble, cope, or dalmatic by the officiating priest and his assistants. {{smaller|It reaches to the feet, and is bound around the waist by a girdle called the ''alb-cord''.
